newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Technology-shy Europe needs liberalised phone lure.
newsitem.headline: Technology-shy Europe needs liberalised phone lure.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent

Liberalised telephone markets will provide cheaper prices and innovative new products, and finally turn Europeans on to the delights of high technology, according to U.S. computer and printer maker Hewlett-Packard Co.

In an interview, H-P's Franz Nawratil, President and Managing Director of the company's Europe, Middle East and Africa division, said European high technology sales growth was slowing, but he remained hopeful of a rally soon.
H-P was being hampered in Europe by the strong dollar.

Nawratil was confident H-P would hold on to its lead in printer markets, and believed there was big mileage in new consumer products like the recently introduced Photosmart system, which allows consumers to take digital pictures and load them directly on to computers.

"There are strong signs that one of the pre-requisites for digital age acceleration in Europe are new telecommunication industries, privatised, deregulated and put into direct competition on a global basis," Nawratil said.

Germany has already moved towards privatising Deutsche Telekom. France Telecom's partial privatisation awaits the green light from the new socialist government. Most European Union markets will begin allowing free competition from January 1, 1998.
Nawratil said that although Europe has lagged behind the U.S. in embracing and producing computer technology, it has led the world in telephone equipment.
Cellular phone technology has been driven on by European companies.

"In telecommunications you will see that Europe is a world leader in technology. A lot of European companies are global players - the Ericssons the Nokias. It's not the same as in the computer industry where you have primarily the US and some Japanese companies who dominate."

Nawratil said he believed a statistic which illustrated the problem was that Europe's per head investment in telecommunications was about the same as in the U.S., although costs here were much higher. But in information technology investment in the U.S. was twice that of western Europe.

The big gap between computer ownership in Europe and the U.S. - more than 40 percent of American households own personal computers compared with less than 20 per cent in Europe - is a big business opportunity for H-P in Europe, according to Nawratil.
Will Europeans, like Americans, get caught up with excitement about the Internet, the world-wide network of personal computers linked by telephone lines?

"Yes, yes it has to be. The expansion of the Internet depends on cheap telephones. For me the telecommunications privatisations, bringing down prices and introducing new services is the base for the computer revolution in Europe. You don't do much with a not-networked computer."
Digital photography will provide new business for H-P.
"We understand inkjet printing very well. We have just introduced printers that can do photo quality type printing, and there I believe is a market which can see expanding into consumer areas."

"With everybody wanting their own Web page, you must have digital photography, and that's something we have introduced just a few weeks ago. It allows you to scan negatives and slides and photos - a camera to take digital photos, then a printer that does photo quality printing under the name of PhotoSmart."
"Like the camcorder market, we believe there will be an amateur digital market out there and we will participate very strongly in it," Nawratil said.
